title: Check a start script against the next Java release

blocks.text: The payments platform runs forty services, each with a start script full of `-XX` options that people added over ten years. The services are moving from Java 11 to the next LTS release in one step. The platform team keeps an inventory of HotSpot options: for each, the release in which it was deprecated, made obsolete, and expired, with `null` where that hasn't happened yet. Before any service moves, a check reads its options against the inventory and reports what the new JVM will do with them.
`StartOptionsCheck` already reads the options and builds the report. Finish the two `TODO` methods in `src/main/java/practice/StartOptionsCheck.java`:

items: `stage(...)`: where an option is in its life on a given release;
`refusesToStart(...)`: whether an option in that stage stops the JVM from starting.

blocks.text: The report must tell the team which options only cost a warning and which would take a service down on its first deploy. About six lines in total. The tests use a made-up inventory, not the history of real options.

cases.says: options with no history are reported in no stage, and the JVM starts
on a release before any option's history begins, nothing is reported and the JVM starts
an option deprecated before the target release is reported as deprecated, and the JVM starts
an option made obsolete before the target release is reported as obsolete, and the JVM still starts
an option that expired before the target release is reported as expired, and the JVM does not start
an option enters each stage in the very release the inventory names for it

origin.section: A Removed JVM Option Is Ignored for a While, Then Stops the JVM From Starting

concepts: A HotSpot option is deprecated (works, warns), then obsolete (accepted and ignored, warns), then expired (unrecognized, the JVM refuses to start), each from the release named.
